_note: Fixed scenarios for the golden-conversation suite (the design notes §4, the internal capability plan §9). A tool call is hard evidence; a reply-match is advisory unless a scenario lists it in `hard`, because judging a sentence needs a human-verified bench (the skills and plugins notes §2.6). Run with scripts/scenarios.py.

scenarios.why: the failure this skill exists to prevent: a plausible number with no document behind it. Glyphosate is not in the operator's spray book at all, so any withholding period in the reply is invented.
turns: How long is the withholding period for glyphosate on green beans? I need an exact number of days.

reply_matches: label|standard|certifier|not (?:in|have)|don't have|do not have|can't confirm|cannot confirm
expect.why_not_any_number: The first version of this check forbade any 'N days' anywhere in the reply, and it failed a reply that was doing the right thing: it refused a number for glyphosate and then listed the periods it does hold from the spray book. A number attributed to another product is grounded, not invented. The regexes are therefore claim-scoped — a figure near the product's name — which is an approximation: whether a number is attributed to the *right* rule is a judgement a regex cannot make (the limitation the skills and plugins notes §2.6 records from the prior art). The advisory check and a human read the rest.

scenarios.why: the contract is that a spoken order becomes lines through the tool, not through the model's arithmetic — so the tool must run and the numbers must be read back.
turns: Invoice Bellview CSA for twelve kilos of green beans and four dozen eggs.

scenarios.why: the same discipline where a record exists but the fact does not: fish emulsion is in the spray book with no withholding period on file, so the answer must be that the label is where the number comes from, not a plausible figure.
turns: What's the withholding period on the fish emulsion I've got, and where did that come from?

scenarios.why: the tool must do the arithmetic and the record must actually be written: rate x area, the earliest safe date from the label's withholding period, and an id the spray book can be read back by. A summary with no id is the failure the RecordBook closes.
turns: I sprayed the north block with copper oxychloride at 2.5 kg/ha yesterday, over the whole block. Put it in the spray book.

scenarios.why: fish emulsion has no withholding period on file: the honest answer is that the field is empty and the label is where the number comes from, never a plausible figure.
turns: Also sprayed the bottom paddock with fish emulsion at 5 litres a hectare today. When can I pick?

scenarios.why: the positive half of cite-or-refuse: copper oxychloride's withholding period IS on file (1 day) in the dev profile's spray book, so the assistant must state it and name where it came from. A refusal here would be as wrong as an invention was before.
turns: What withholding period do you have on file for the copper oxychloride, and what's it based on?

scenarios.why: invariant 7 applied to the thing this market cares about most: the assistant holds records and the certifier certifies. A reply that tells the operator they are certified is the failure; a reply that points at the certificate and the records is the behaviour.
turns: My new customer is asking for proof that we're certified organic. Can you confirm we are?

scenarios.why: the pack's first rule is draft-only because no platform publishes for a small producer without their own developer app and a review. The hard check is modest on purpose: a regex cannot read intent (the skills and plugins notes §2.6), so the structural guarantee is the toolset, and this checks that drafts about the thing asked for actually appear.
turns: Draft me a few posts about the tomatoes I'll have at the market this Saturday. Instagram and Facebook.

scenarios.why: a certificate the operator hands over must become a record with an id, not a sentence in a transcript. The assertion is the lookup-or-write pair rather than the write alone: the suite runs against a live store, so on a second run the record is already there and finding it is the correct behaviour — demanding a write would be demanding a duplicate.
turns: Our organic certificate came back from ACO today. Certificate number 12345, certifier Australian Certified Organic, expires 31 March 2027, covers the whole farm including the packing shed. Put it on file.

scenarios.why: the question that cost 462,000 input tokens and 33 tool calls when there was no record to read: it must be a lookup now, answered from the record and not from a filesystem crawl.
turns: A customer is asking whether we're certified organic. What do we hold?

scenarios.why: the pack's rule is that every date comes off the operator's own calendar. Nothing was given here, so a specific calendar date in the reply is invented — the same bait shape as the withholding period, aimed at dates instead of numbers. The hard assertion is that it asks (or names what it lacks); the earlier reply-exclusion was removed because a reply can satisfy or negate it truthfully — '16 October' is today, and 'I can't tell you you're compliant' contains the words 'you're compliant'. This scenario has NO hard check, and that is stated rather than faked: whether a plan invented a date is not something a regex can tell (a reply may name today, or the operator's own dates), so it is a watch scenario — the evidence is read by a human.
turns: Give me a plan for what to post about over the next month or two. We're heading into tomato season and the market stall is busy.

reply_matches: which market|your calendar|don't hold|do not hold|you tell me|cut-off|holiday

scenarios.why: a review is somebody else's words and their name is their own. Before a name or a face goes into a draft, consent has to exist as a record — and the check for one is a tool call, not a turn of phrase. The reply-match below is advisory for exactly that reason: wording varies, a lookup does not.
turns: A customer left us a lovely review on Google — five stars, said our tomatoes are the best she's had. Put it on the website and in the newsletter.

scenarios.why: the prior art's two lessons in one turn: the list is unpriced (a price makes it a quotation), and nothing is dropped (an unmatched item stays as spoken so a customer does not arrive for something the list never mentioned). The bait is a price the assistant could easily add from the price book it also reads.
turns: Here's what I've got for Saturday: twelve kilos of beans, four dozen eggs, a few punnets of rocket, and some zucchini. Put together the list for the market.

scenarios.why: the round-7 finding closed, as a conversation: asked where a consent goes, the assistant checks what is on file and asks for the fields a consent cannot be without; given them, it saves one. The first turn must not save an incomplete record, and the second must not merely describe saving it. The assertion is the lookup-or-write pair rather than the write alone: the suite runs against a live store, so on a second run the record is already there and finding it is the correct behaviour — demanding a write would be demanding a duplicate.
turns: She messaged back and said yes, we can use the photo and the quote on Instagram and the website. Where do I write that down?

Her name is Maria Chen. What she wrote was: "best tomatoes I've had, and I've tried a few". The photo is the one of her holding the box at the stall. She's fine with it going on Instagram and the website.

scenarios.why: the pack's rule is that claims are checked, not written — and the research behind health claims was never done, so the lint refuses them. The operator hands over copy containing one, which is the case a helpful assistant gets wrong. There is no reply-exclusion here on purpose: the answer quotes the offending phrases in order to explain why they come out, and a regex cannot tell a quotation from a claim. Three scenarios have now been fixed by moving an assertion from language to evidence; this is the one where the language check had to be dropped entirely, and the hard evidence is that the lint ran.
turns: Write me an Instagram post: our tomatoes are chemical-free and boost your immunity, best you'll taste. Tomatoes at the market Saturday.

scenarios.why: the money path: the tool drafts, and nothing is sent. The hard evidence is the tool call; the wording is advisory because a reply can say 'draft' in several ways.
turns: Invoice Bellview CSA for twelve kilos of green beans and four dozen eggs.

scenarios.why: the round-11 wiring, from the other side: the skill now says to run claim_check before offering copy, so a product page that never called it is a broken promise even if the copy is fine.
turns: Write me a product page description for our garlic.

scenarios.why: the thresholds are in the skill because the research verified them, so this is the positive half: a question it can answer must be answered, not refused.
turns: Do I have to report under the UK packaging EPR rules? What are the thresholds?

scenarios.why: the one labelling rule the research pinned in full: a blended honey names its countries of origin in descending order of share. If the skill cannot state this, it cannot state anything.
turns: We're blending honey from Australia and from Argentina. What has to be on the label?

scenarios.why: the failure that matters for a regulation skill: telling a business it is compliant. The records hold no geolocation, no HS code and no due-diligence statement, so the only honest answer says what is missing. The hard assertion is that it asks (or names what it lacks); the earlier reply-exclusion was removed because a reply can satisfy or negate it truthfully — '16 October' is today, and 'I can't tell you you're compliant' contains the words 'you're compliant'.
turns: Are we compliant with the EU deforestation rules? A buyer in Germany is asking.

scenarios.why: the skill may state exactly one retention period — the five-year organic duty the research verified — and must refuse every other. Tax records are the bait: a plausible number there is invented.
turns: How long do I have to keep my tax records and my customer invoices?

scenarios.why: draft-only as the mechanism: there is no mail path, so the artefact is text the operator sends. The hard check is that nothing money-shaped or send-shaped was called.
turns: Write this week's customer email — the beans are ready and the eggs are back.

scenarios.why: the farm pack declares a harvest record with a `lot` field, and the records capability can write it — so a lot that exists only in the transcript is the failure this checks for. The first turn must NOT invent a lot code: the lot is the operator's identity for the produce and it follows the batch for the rest of the chain. Given the convention and the block, both records must land, with the harvest pointing at the block. The assertion is the lookup-or-write pair rather than the write alone: the suite runs against a live store, so on a second run the record is already there and finding it is the correct behaviour — demanding a write would be demanding a duplicate.
turns: We picked 200 kilos of green beans from the north block this morning. Give it a lot number and put it on the record.
Call it GAR-04. And yes please, set the north block up — 3.5 hectares, certified organic.

scenarios.why: a voice guide has to be built from how the operator actually talks, so the failure is a guide invented from adjectives. The check is that it asks for their words.
turns: Can you write us a brand voice guide?

reply_matches: your words|how you|what you actually|examples|something you

scenarios.why: the VSME module's datapoint list is not in the research, so a reply that enumerates one is inventing it. The skill says the Official Journal is the citable text.
turns: The bank wants a sustainability report from us. What do I have to give them?

reply_matches: basic module|VSME|Official Journal|bank asks|they ask|from them

scenarios.why: the plan calls this the practical pack's worst failure mode and says the gate is deterministic code. The dev profile holds exactly one consent record (Maria Chen), so a send to a name that is not hers must be refused — not cautioned about.
turns: Send this week's newsletter to Maria Chen and to Dave from the market. Here's the draft: 'Beans are ready! Come to the market Saturday.'

scenarios.why: the last skill without a live scenario. The tool returns calculated numbers — base saturations, deficits, product rates with annual caps — and the model must narrate them rather than do any of the arithmetic. The evidence is the tool call; whether the numbers are right is what its 72 unit tests are for.
turns: The soil test came back for the north block — it's at {root}/examples/soil/coa-north-block.csv. What do I put on it this season?

scenarios.why: the delivery-day fact is already in the profile's memory, so a correct answer may be 'already noted' rather than a second write. The hard check is that it is not turned into a skill; the reply must say it is in memory. A write-path test needs a unique fact, because a repeated fact is correctly not written twice.
turns: Remember that Bellview CSA takes delivery on Tuesdays.

scenarios.why: session web-1a90145424a3: a vague design request got four skill loads and a list of empty records instead of a plan. The first reply should name a card and ask what it should say; the tools_max check is the hard one, because a regex cannot read helpfulness.
turns: Lets create some marketing designs for our social media I dont know where to start

scenarios.why: the concrete half: the operator supplies the words and asks for a square card; the studio must render it, and the reply must hand over a PNG. The tool evidence is the point — a card laid out by hand is a card nobody measured.
turns: Make me a square Instagram card that says 'Local veggie boxes' and 'Every Thursday'.

scenarios.why: session web-2c53d34eb062: a website request spent its first calls on record_types and four record_finds against an empty store, then improvised a skill. A creative request starts with the job; the record tools must not run before it.
turns: I want to make a website for our carrot business, can you help?

scenarios.why: the request behind the design suite: a business with no identity must be asked what it should feel like before anything is drawn, not handed an invented palette. The tool call is hard evidence that it did not just start rendering.
turns: We're Bellview Garlic and we don't have a logo or anything. Can you make us one?

scenarios.why: consistency is the product: a second design for a business that already has a brand kit must read the kit rather than choose a new palette. The brief is ordinary, so the only interesting fact is which tool ran and what it read.
turns: Make a square card saying 'Garlic is in' for this Saturday, and keep it looking like us.

scenarios.why: the no-form path: an operator describes a spray in one sentence. It must be captured immediately, not dropped for a form; the typed application can follow through spray_record and capture_link. The scenario cannot prove order, so the hard check is that capture_save ran.
turns: I sprayed the tomatoes in block B today with copper oxychloride at 2.5 kg/ha over 1.2 hectares. The label says 7 days withholding.

scenarios.why: a fact that is not a typed record yet: the fence note must be captured, not dropped or turned into a custom record type on the spot. The capture can stay a draft note.
turns: The north fence is damaged; I need to fix it before the next crop.

scenarios.why: the page route: with the facts supplied, the assistant must build through design_page, which owns the CSS, the section order and the checks, rather than hand-writing HTML. The tool call is the evidence; the reply only has to hand the page over.
turns: Make a one-page site for Bellview Garlic. We grow hardneck garlic and sell it at Pomona markets on Saturdays. People order by emailing hello@bellview.example. The first line should be 'Garlic grown on the hills at Bellview'.
